(Benefit)

Sleep has two benefits:

The first: the heat is redirected to the belly, so that food is digested.

The second: the rest of the limbs that have grown weary from their activities.

(Faʾida)

The grammarians differ over whether a condition of the disjunctive exception (al-istithnāʾ al-munqaṭiʿ) is that it must be possible to consider it included in the thing excepted from in some way, or whether this is not a condition.

Many grammarians did not stipulate this, while others did stipulate it.

Ibn al-Sarrāj said: "When the exception is disjunctive, it is necessary that the preceding statement, before (illā), indicate what is excepted."

According to the first view, no estimation is needed.

According to the second view, it is necessary to estimate a return (al-radd), and let us mention examples of this:

His Exalted saying: ﴿They will remain therein for ages, tasting therein neither coolness nor drink, except boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid﴾

On the view of not estimating inclusion (al-tanāwul), the statement is the negation of one thing and the affirmation of its opposite, which is more evident.

On the view of estimating inclusion: since the tasting of coolness and drink was negated, it might be supposed that they taste nothing other than these two, so He said ﴿except boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid﴾.

Thus the exception is from an estimated general term.

He said in (al-Madārij):

The criterion of the disjunctive exception is that it has inclusion within the genus of the thing excepted from, even if it is not included in itself and its wording does not encompass it, such as His saying ﴿They hear therein no vain talk, except the word "Peace"﴾ [Maryam: 62].

For "peace" is included in the speech that is the genus of vain talk and peace. Likewise His saying: ﴿They taste therein neither coolness nor drink, except boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid﴾ [al-Naba: 24].

For boiling water and the dark liquid are included in the genus of tasting, which is divided, as if it were said in the first: "They hear therein nothing except peace," and in the second: "They taste therein nothing except boiling water and dark, pus-like liquid." He specified one individual from the individuals of the genus explicitly, so that its negation is by way of explicit specification, not by way of generality, which admits the specification of this individual.

(Faṣl)

Al-Suddī said, concerning His saying ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾: he said, "Seven hundred ages (ḥuqb), each age being seventy years, each year being three hundred and sixty days, each day being like a thousand years of what you count."

The restriction of their remaining therein to ages indicates a determined period limited by number.

This is the view of the majority. For this reason al-Zajjāj interpreted the verse as making the ages a restriction of His saying ﴿they taste therein neither coolness nor drink﴾.

As for the duration of their stay therein, it is not determined by ages.

This interpretation is corrupt, for it implies that after the ages they would be tasting coolness and drink.

Another group said the verse is abrogated by His saying ﴿they are not to be brought out of it﴾ and His saying ﴿they will abide therein forever﴾.

This is also corrupt if by abrogation they mean removal (al-rafʿ), for that does not apply to a report unless it has the sense of a command. If by abrogation they mean clarification (al-bayān), then it is sound, and it only indicates that their punishment is lasting and continuous as long as they remain: ﴿they abide therein forever﴾ and ﴿they are not to be brought out﴾.

This is a known truth, indicated by the Qur'an and the Sunnah, but the matter at issue is another: that the Fire is everlasting and perpetual as long as the Lord endures. Where is the evidence for this from the Qur'an or the Sunnah in any way whatsoever?

Another group said it refers to the people of monotheism (ahl al-tawḥīd).

This is uglier than what preceded it, and the context of the verses rejects it outright.

When others saw the invalidity of these interpretations, one said: the mention of ages does not indicate an end, for they are not determined by a number; He did not say ten or a hundred. Even if they were determined by number, it would indicate an end only by implication, so how much more so when they are not determined?

They said the meaning of the verse is that whenever one age passes, another follows it, without end.

The verse does not indicate this in any way. As for their claim that the ages therein are not determined: it is said that if the verse were intended to show that the duration of the punishment does not end, it would not have been restricted to ages, for what has no end is not described as lasting "ages, eons, and aeons" or the like.

For this reason one does not say this about the bliss of the people of Paradise, nor does one say of the everlasting, which does not cease, that it lasts "ages" or "thousands of years." The Companions understood the Qur'an's meanings better, and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb understood from it a meaning contrary to the understanding of these people, just as Ibn ʿAbbās understood from the verse of exception a meaning contrary to theirs. The understanding of the Companions regarding the Qur'an is the ultimate reference on which one relies.

Ibn Masʿūd said: "There will come upon Hell a time when its doors will slam, with no one in it, and that is after they have remained in it for ages."

Ibn Jarīr said: a report from al-Musayyib, from one whom he named, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning ﴿abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord wills﴾: he said, "God commanded the Fire to consume them."

He said: and Ibn Masʿūd said the same, and he mentioned it. He said: Muḥammad ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us: Jarīr narrated to us from Bayān, from al-Shaʿbī, who said:

"Hell is the quicker of the two abodes to be built and the quicker to be ruined."

I say: His saying "the quicker to be ruined" does not indicate the ruin of the other abode, as in His saying: ﴿The companions of Paradise on that day are better in their resting place and finer in their place of repose﴾ and His saying: ﴿Is God better, or what they associate?﴾

And in the hadith: "God is higher and greater." And "the quicker to be built" may have two meanings:

One: the people's haste toward the deeds by which they enter Hell, and their slowness toward the deeds of the Hereafter.

The second: that its people enter it before the people of Paradise enter it, for the people of Paradise enter it only after crossing the Ṣirāṭ and being detained at the bridge beyond it, whereas the people of the Fire have already taken up their places in it, for they do not cross the Ṣirāṭ nor are they detained at that bridge.

He said in (Ḥādī al-Arwāḥ), with the following text:

The seventh: the view of one who says that rather, its Lord and Creator, blessed and exalted, will annihilate it, for He has set for it a term at which it ends, after which it will perish and its punishment will cease.

Shaykh al-Islām said: this view has been reported from ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd, Abū Hurayra, Abū Saʿīd and others. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, one of the greatest imams of hadith, has related in his well-known Tafsir: Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb narrated to us: Ḥammād ibn Salama narrated to us, from Thābit, from al-Ḥasan, who said: ʿUmar said: "If the people of the Fire remained in the Fire as long as the sands of ʿĀlij, there would still be for them a day on which they would come out."

He also said: Ḥajjāj ibn Minhāl narrated to us, from Ḥammād ibn Salama, from Ḥumayd, from al-Ḥasan, that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: "If the people of the Fire remained in the Fire the number of the sands of ʿĀlij, there would still be for them a day on which they come out of it." He mentioned this in the tafsir of His saying ﴿remaining therein for ages﴾.

ʿAbd, who is among the imams, the memorizers, and the scholars of the Sunnah, related it from these two eminent men, Sulaymān ibn Ḥarb and Ḥajjāj ibn Minhāl, and both of them from Ḥammād ibn Salama, and that is sufficient in its eminence. Ḥammād narrates it from Thābit and Ḥumayd, and both of them narrate it from al-Ḥasan, and this chain is sufficient in its eminence. Although al-Ḥasan did not hear from ʿUmar, he related it from some of the Successors, and if it were not authentic to him he would not have stated it firmly as "ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said." Even if it were not established from ʿUmar, the continued transmission of these imams without opposing it or rejecting it, while they denounce those who oppose the Sunnah even without this, shows that if this view were among the innovations contrary to the Book of God, the Sunnah of His Messenger, and the consensus of the imams, they would have been the first to reject it.

He said: There is no doubt that whoever says this view and reports it from ʿUmar intended by it the kind of the people of the Fire who are its people. As for those afflicted for their sins, these and others know that they will come out of it, and that they will not remain the sands of ʿĀlij nor anything close to it. The term "people of the Fire" is not restricted to the monotheists; rather it is restricted to others, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "As for the people of the Fire who are its people, they neither die therein nor live." This is not contradicted by His saying ﴿abiding therein﴾ and His saying ﴿nor are they to be brought out of it﴾.

Rather, what God has reported is the truth and the reality that cannot be opposed. But when its term ends and it perishes, the world perishes, it will no longer be a fire, and no punishment will remain in it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 78, verses 31–33:

*Fa-l-kawā'ib* (ﷻ): the plural of *kā'ib*, which means *nāhid* (a maiden whose breasts are firm and rounded). This is the view of Qatadah, Mujahid and the exegetes generally.

Al-Kalbi said: they are the *falakāt*, the young women whose breasts are rounded (*taka''aba thadyuhunna*), and *tafalakat* (meaning the same).

The root of the word comes from the idea of roundness (*al-istidārah*).

The meaning is that their breasts are firm (*nawāhid*), like pomegranates, not hanging downward; and they are called *nawāhid* and *kawā'ib*.

(Benefit)
